lessons.title: Calculating Food Costs
lessons.body: To price your catering, you must first know exactly what each dish costs to make. Start by listing every ingredient for a recipe. For example, a pot of jollof rice for 20 people might need 5 cups of rice (1 cup = 200g, so 1kg), 1 litre of oil, 6 large tomatoes, 2 onions, 1 tin of tomato paste, spices, and 1kg of chicken. Next, find the current market price for each item. If rice is 1,200 KES per kg, oil is 300 KES per litre, tomatoes are 100 KES, onions 50 KES, tomato paste 150 KES, spices 100 KES, and chicken 500 KES, your total food cost is 2,400 KES. Divide by 20 servings: each serving costs 120 KES in ingredients. Always add a 10% buffer for price changes and wasteâso use 132 KES per serving. Use a simple notebook or a free app like 'Food Cost Calculator' to track. Remember, prices vary by season and location; update your costs monthly. This number is the foundation for setting your menu price. Without it, you might charge too little and lose money, or too much and lose customers.

lessons.title: Labor and Overhead Expenses
lessons.body: Food is not your only cost. You must pay yourself and cover overheads. Labor includes your time and any helpers. Decide an hourly rate. In Nairobi, a caterer might pay themselves 300 KES per hour. If a job takes 8 hours, that's 2,400 KES. If you hire one helper at 200 KES per hour for 6 hours, that's 1,200 KES. Total labor: 3,600 KES. Overhead includes gas, electricity, water, transport, packaging, and equipment wear. For a small event, estimate: gas 500 KES, electricity 200 KES, water 100 KES, transport 800 KES, packaging (foil pans, lids, bags) 600 KES. Total overhead: 2,200 KES. Add these to your food cost. If food cost was 2,400 KES, total direct costs = 2,400 + 3,600 + 2,200 = 8,200 KES. For 20 servings, that's 410 KES per serving. But you also have fixed monthly costs like rent, internet, and phone. If your monthly fixed costs are 10,000 KES and you do 4 events per month, allocate 2,500 KES per event. So total cost per event = 8,200 + 2,500 = 10,700 KES. This is your break-even point. Any price above this gives profit.

lessons.title: Setting Profitable Prices
lessons.body: Now that you know your total cost per event, you can set a price that earns a profit. A common method is cost-plus pricing: add a markup percentage to your total cost. For catering, a 30-50% markup is standard. If your total cost is 10,700 KES, a 40% markup gives 10,700 x 1.4 = 14,980 KES. Round to 15,000 KES. That means each of 20 servings is 750 KES. Check if this is competitive. If similar caterers charge 800 KES per serving, you are slightly cheaper. If they charge 600 KES, you may need to reduce costs or accept lower profit. Another method is value-based pricing: consider what clients are willing to pay for your unique dishes or service. For a wedding, you might charge more. Always calculate your profit margin: (Price - Cost) / Price x 100. For 15,000 KES price and 10,700 KES cost, profit = 4,300 KES, margin = 28.7%. Aim for at least 20% margin. Never price below cost. Use a simple spreadsheet or notebook to test different prices and see the profit. Adjust based on demand and feedback.

lessons.title: Creating Quotes and Invoices
lessons.body: A quote is a document you give a potential client showing what you will provide and the price. An invoice is a bill you send after the event (or before, if you require deposit). Both should be professional and clear. Use a free tool like Wave, Zoho Invoice, or even a Word template. Include: your business name, contact, client name, date, event date, description of services (e.g., 'Jollof rice, chicken, salad for 20 people'), quantity, unit price, total, and any terms. For example: 20 servings x 750 KES = 15,000 KES. Add a line for deposit required (e.g., 50% = 7,500 KES). State payment methods: M-Pesa, bank transfer, cash. For quotes, add an expiry date (e.g., 'Valid for 14 days'). For invoices, add an invoice number and due date. Always keep a copy. Send via email or WhatsApp as a PDF. A clear quote builds trust and reduces disputes. If a client asks for changes, update the quote and resend. Never start cooking without a signed quote or written confirmation.

lessons.title: Payment Terms and Deposits
lessons.body: To protect your business, always take a deposit before buying ingredients. A standard deposit is 50% of the total. For a 15,000 KES event, ask for 7,500 KES upfront. This covers your initial costs and ensures the client is serious. The remaining 50% is due on the event day, before or immediately after delivery. For larger events (over 50,000 KES), you might ask for 60% deposit and 40% on delivery. Clearly state your payment terms in the quote and invoice: '50% deposit required to confirm booking. Balance due on delivery.' Accept mobile money (M-Pesa, Airtel Money), bank transfer, or cash. Always issue a receipt for the deposit. If a client cancels within 7 days of the event, you may keep the deposit to cover costs already incurred. For cancellations earlier, you might refund part of the deposit. Put these terms in writing. Late payments: add a clause like 'Late payments incur 5% fee per week.' This encourages timely payment. Never let a client owe you more than the deposit; if they don't pay the balance, you can withhold the food. Be firm but polite.

lessons.title: Tracking Income and Expenses
lessons.body: To know if your catering business is profitable, track every shilling in and out. Use a simple notebook or a free app like 'Money Manager' or a spreadsheet. Record each sale: date, client, event, amount received. Record each expense: date, item, amount, category (food, labor, transport, etc.). For example, on 1st June, you earn 15,000 KES from a wedding. On 2nd June, you spend 2,400 KES on food, 1,200 KES on helper, 800 KES on transport. At month's end, total income minus total expenses = profit. If income is 60,000 KES and expenses 45,000 KES, profit is 15,000 KES. Separate business and personal money. Open a separate bank account or mobile wallet for the business. Keep receipts for all purchases. Every month, review your numbers: which dishes are most profitable? Where can you cut costs? Use this to adjust prices. Also set aside 10% of profit for taxes and emergencies. Tracking helps you make informed decisions and grow sustainably.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Pricing, Budgeting, and Financials for Home-Based Catering

In home-based catering across Africa, the difference between a business that survives and one that thrives is rarely the quality of the food alone. It is the discipline of the numbers. Whether you are cooking for a 30-person wedding in Kumasi, a corporate lunch in Nairobi, or a naming ceremony in Lagos, your ability to calculate costs, price profitably, and track every shilling, naira, or cedi determines whether you build wealth or merely stay busy. This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in this module into a working toolkit you can apply immediately.

1. Calculating Food Costs

Food cost is the single largest expense in most home-based catering operations, typically representing 30â45% of revenue. The mistake most caterers make is estimating costs from memory rather than recording them. You must calculate cost per portion, not cost per pot.

The formula: Total ingredient cost Ã· number of portions = food cost per portion. Then multiply by the number of guests to get total food cost for an event.

Always add a waste and shrinkage allowance of 5â10%. Rice expands, meat trims down, and vegetables spoil. In markets where you buy from open-air vendorsâcommon across West and East Africaâprices fluctuate weekly with season and fuel costs, so update your costing sheet before every quote.

2. Labor and Overhead Expenses

Home-based caterers frequently undercharge because they forget to pay themselves. Your labor is a real cost. If you hire one assistant for a 12-hour event day, that is a direct labor cost. Even if you cook alone, assign a notional wage to your own hoursâthis protects your business from appearing more profitable than it is.

Overhead includes everything not tied to a single dish: gas or charcoal, electricity, water, transport to market, packaging, disposable plates and cutlery, phone data for client coordination, and equipment depreciation (pots, coolers, gas cylinders). In many African cities, transport and fuel alone can add 10â15% to your total cost.

Table 1: Typical cost structure for a home-based catering event (percentage of total cost)
Cost Category Typical Range Notes
Food ingredients35â45%Varies with menu and market
Direct labor15â25%Includes your own time
Fuel and energy5â10%Gas, charcoal, electricity
Transport and logistics5â12%Market runs and delivery
Packaging and disposables3â8%Containers, cutlery, napkins
Equipment depreciation2â5%Set aside for replacement
Profit margin15â25%Your reward and buffer

Source: Adapted from ILO Start and Improve Your Business (SIYB) costing guidance and TechnoServe Africa food enterprise training materials (2021).

3. Setting Profitable Prices

There are three pricing methods. Use all three and compare:

  • Cost-plus pricing: Total cost per portion Ã (1 + markup). If cost per portion is 800 KES and you want a 40% margin, price at 1,120 KES.
  • Market-based pricing: What do comparable caterers charge in your city? Stay within 10â15% unless your quality or brand justifies more.
  • Value-based pricing: What is the event worth to the client? A wedding client may pay more per head than a funeral client for the same menu.

Never price below cost. A common trap is winning a large event at a low price and losing money on volume. If a client's budget is below your cost, reduce the menu scopeânot your price.

4. Creating Quotes and Invoices

A professional quote wins trust. Include: your business name and contact, client name, event date and venue, number of guests, menu items with per-head price, additional services (serving staff, rentals, delivery), subtotal, deposit required, balance due date, and validity period (typically 7â14 days).

An invoice is issued after the event or upon deposit. It must reference the quote number, list what was delivered, show payments received, and state the outstanding balance. In many African markets, handwritten invoices are acceptable, but a printed or PDF invoice signals professionalism and helps with record-keeping.

5. Payment Terms and Deposits

Cash flow kills more small caterers than bad cooking. Protect yourself with clear terms:

  • Deposit: 50% upfront is standard. For large events (100+ guests), request 60â70%.
  • Balance: Due on delivery or within 7 days of invoice.
  • Cancellation: State clearly that deposits are non-refundable within 7 days of the event, since you will have already purchased ingredients.
  • Accepted methods: Mobile money (M-Pesa, MTN MoMo, Airtel Money), bank transfer, or cash with receipt.
â  SAFETY & FINANCIAL WARNING:

Never begin shopping or cooking for an event without a confirmed deposit in hand. Verbal promises are not payment. In cash-heavy markets, insist on mobile money or bank transfer so you have a written record. Do not accept post-dated cheques from new clients. If a client refuses any deposit, decline the jobâthis is the single most common cause of caterer bankruptcy across Africa.

6. Tracking Income and Expenses

You cannot grow what you do not measure. Keep two simple records:

  • Income log: Date, client, event, amount received, payment method, balance outstanding.
  • Expense log: Date, item, category (food, labor, transport, packaging, equipment), amount, receipt number.

A notebook works, but a simple spreadsheet (Google Sheets or Excel) on your phone is better because it calculates totals automatically. At month-end, subtract expenses from income to find your profit. Set aside 20â30% of profit for equipment replacement and slow seasons.

Table 2: Sample monthly income and expense tracker (illustrative figures in KES)
Item Category Amount Running Balance
Deposit â Wedding (80 guests)Income+40,00040,000
Market â rice, meat, spicesFoodâ18,50021,500
Assistant cook (2 days)Laborâ4,00017,500
Transport â market & venueLogisticsâ2,20015,300
Gas refillFuelâ2,80012,500
Disposable plates & cutleryPackagingâ3,0009,500
Balance â WeddingIncome+40,00049,500
Corporate lunch (25 guests)Income+18,00067,500

Source: Format adapted from the ILO's Financial Education: Manage Your Money workbook and GIZ SME bookkeeping templates used in East African micro-enterprise training (2020).

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Update market prices for every ingredient before quotingânever use last month's figures.
  2. Calculate cost per portion, then add 5â10% for waste and shrinkage.
  3. Include your own labor time as a cost, even if you are not paying yourself cash.
  4. Add fuel, transport, packaging, and equipment depreciation to every quote.
  5. Set a price that gives you at least a 15â25% profit margin after all costs.
  6. Issue a written quote with a validity period and require a 50% deposit before shopping.
  7. Record every income and expense the same day it happensâno exceptions.
  8. Review your profit monthly and set aside 20â30% for equipment and slow seasons.

Further Reading

  • ILO â Start and Improve Your Business (SIYB) Programme Materials (free business and costing guides)
  • FAO â Small-Scale Food Processing Enterprise Guide (free PDF on costing and enterprise planning)
  • TechnoServe â Entrepreneurship Resources (free tools for African food businesses)
  • GIZ â Financial Literacy Training Manual (free bookkeeping and cash-flow modules)
  • African Development Bank â SME Knowledge Publications (free reports on African small enterprise finance)

Bottom line: In home-based catering, your food brings the client, but your numbers keep the business alive. Master costing, price with confidence, protect yourself with deposits, and track every transaction. That is how a home kitchen becomes a real African enterprise.

quiz.q: What is the first step in calculating food costs?
options: B) List all ingredients for a recipe
quiz.explanation: You must know what goes into a dish before you can cost it.

quiz.q: If a recipe for 20 people costs 2,400 KES in ingredients, what is the cost per serving?
quiz.explanation: 2,400 divided by 20 equals 120 KES per serving.

quiz.q: Why add a 10% buffer to food costs?
options: A) To cover price changes and waste
quiz.explanation: A buffer accounts for unexpected variations in prices and spoilage.

quiz.q: Which of these is an overhead expense?
quiz.explanation: Gas is an indirect cost, not a direct food ingredient.

quiz.q: If you pay yourself 300 KES per hour and work 8 hours, what is your labor cost?
quiz.explanation: 300 multiplied by 8 equals 2,400 KES.

quiz.q: What is the break-even point?
options: A) The price at which you make maximum profit
B) The total cost of an event
C) The price at which you cover all costs
quiz.explanation: Break-even is when income equals total costs, resulting in zero profit.

quiz.q: If total cost per event is 10,700 KES and you use a 40% markup, what is the selling price?
quiz.explanation: 10,700 multiplied by 1.4 equals 14,980 KES.

quiz.q: What is a good profit margin to aim for in catering?
quiz.explanation: A margin of at least 20% ensures sustainability and growth.

quiz.q: Which document shows a potential client what you will provide and the price?
quiz.explanation: A quote is a formal offer before the job is confirmed.

quiz.q: What should be included in an invoice?
options: B) Invoice number and due date
quiz.explanation: Invoices need unique numbers and due dates for tracking and payment.

quiz.q: What is a common deposit percentage for catering?
quiz.explanation: A 50% deposit is standard to cover initial costs and secure the booking.

quiz.q: When is the balance typically due?
options: A) One month after the event
D) When the client feels like it
quiz.explanation: The remaining balance is usually paid on delivery or the event day.

quiz.q: What should you do if a client cancels within 7 days of the event?
quiz.explanation: The deposit compensates for costs already incurred and lost opportunities.

quiz.q: Why is it important to track income and expenses?
options: A) To know your profit and make informed decisions
quiz.explanation: Tracking shows profitability and helps adjust prices and costs.

quiz.q: Which tool can help you track finances for free?
quiz.explanation: All these can be used, but apps offer more features.

quiz.q: What percentage of profit should you set aside for taxes and emergencies?
quiz.explanation: Setting aside 10% helps cover unexpected costs and tax obligations.

quiz.q: If your monthly income is 60,000 KES and expenses are 45,000 KES, what is your profit?
quiz.explanation: 60,000 minus 45,000 equals 15,000 KES profit.

quiz.q: What is a fixed monthly cost?
options: C) Gas for a specific event
quiz.explanation: Rent is a cost that does not change with the number of events.

quiz.q: How do you calculate profit margin?
quiz.explanation: This formula gives the percentage of profit relative to the price.

quiz.q: What is value-based pricing?
options: A) Pricing based on cost plus markup
B) Pricing based on what clients are willing to pay
C) Pricing based on competitor prices
D) Pricing based on random choice
quiz.explanation: Value-based pricing considers the perceived value to the customer.

quiz.q: Why should you never price below cost?
options: C) Clients will not respect you
D) It is too much work
quiz.explanation: Pricing below cost means you pay to work, leading to losses.

quiz.q: What should you do before starting to cook for an event?
options: B) Get a signed quote or written confirmation
quiz.explanation: Written confirmation protects you from clients who might cancel or dispute.

quiz.q: What is a receipt used for?
options: B) To prove payment was made
quiz.explanation: A receipt is proof that a payment has been received.

quiz.q: If a client owes you more than the deposit, what can you do?
quiz.explanation: You can legally withhold delivery until payment is made, as per your terms.

quiz.q: What is a good way to separate business and personal money?
options: B) Open a separate business account
C) Keep cash in a drawer
quiz.explanation: A separate account makes tracking and tax filing easier.

quiz.q: What should you review monthly to improve your business?
quiz.explanation: Monthly financial review helps identify profitable dishes and cost-saving opportunities.

quiz.q: Which of these is a direct cost for a catering event?
quiz.explanation: Chicken is a direct ingredient used in the dishes for the event.

quiz.q: If you hire a helper for 6 hours at 200 KES per hour, what is the labor cost?
quiz.explanation: 6 multiplied by 200 equals 1,200 KES.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a quote expiry date?
options: B) To limit the validity of the offered price
C) To show you are busy
quiz.explanation: An expiry date protects you from cost changes after a certain period.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep receipts for all purchases?
options: A) For tax purposes and tracking
D) To remember what you bought
quiz.explanation: Receipts are essential for accurate expense tracking and tax deductions.
